		<title><![CDATA[What is a self managed super fund? A Practical Guide to SMSFs]]></title>
		<link>https://tnaccounting.com.au/?p=14624</link>
		<pubDate></pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[xdilvx]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://tnaccounting.com.au/?p=14624</guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Think of your superannuation. For most of us, it’s something that happens in the background. Money goes in, someone else manages it, and hopefully, it grows. A Self Managed Super Fund (SMSF) flips that entire model on its head.</p>
<p>An SMSF puts you firmly in the driver&#039;s seat of your retirement savings. Instead of being a passenger in a large, professionally managed fund, you become the one making all the key decisions about where your super is invested. It’s a move from passive saving to actively building your own financial future.</p>
<h2>Understanding the Basics of an SMSF</h2>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdn.outrank.so/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/83a771f4-e192-4dd2-9afc-1f268c8aa523/what-is-a-self-managed-super-fund-super-fund.jpg" alt="Mature couple reviewing documents and using a laptop at a kitchen table, with an &#039;SMSF&#039; sign." /></figure></p>
<p>So, what exactly <em>is</em> a self managed super fund in practice? At its heart, an SMSF is your own private super fund, set up under a specific legal structure—a trust. This trust is established for one reason and one reason only: to provide retirement benefits for its members.</p>
<p>This structure allows you and up to <strong>five</strong> other people to pool your super together. The critical rule is that all members must also be trustees (or directors of a corporate trustee). This means everyone is on the hook, jointly responsible for every decision and for keeping the fund compliant with Australian law.</p>
<h3>The Shift from Member to Trustee</h3>
<p>The biggest mental and practical shift when you start an SMSF is your change in role. In a standard industry or retail fund, you’re simply a member. Your money gets invested by a fund manager you’ve likely never met. With an SMSF, you wear two hats: you&#039;re both a <strong>member</strong> and a <strong>trustee</strong>.</p>
<p>This dual responsibility is what gives you such powerful control. You&#039;re no longer picking from a limited menu of investment options. Instead, the whole investment universe opens up, allowing you to build a portfolio that’s perfectly aligned with your specific goals.</p>
<p>This control breaks down into a few key areas:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Direct investment choice:</strong> You get to decide exactly what to invest in—be it specific shares, commercial property, term deposits, or alternative assets.</li>
<li><strong>Strategic direction:</strong> You are legally required to create and stick to a formal <strong>investment strategy</strong>. This document maps out your goals, risk tolerance, and how you plan to achieve your retirement objectives.</li>
<li><strong>Hands-on management:</strong> You’re now responsible for the day-to-day running of the fund. This includes everything from meticulous record-keeping to ensuring every decision complies with complex superannuation laws.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Who Is an SMSF Suitable For?</h3>
<p>While total control sounds fantastic, an SMSF is definitely not for everyone. It’s a serious commitment that demands your time, a decent level of financial literacy, and a willingness to shoulder significant legal responsibilities. It’s usually a better fit for people who have a clear vision for their retirement and the confidence to make it happen.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>An SMSF gives you the keys to your retirement vehicle. You choose the destination, the route, and the speed, but you&#039;re also responsible for the maintenance and ensuring you follow the rules of the road.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>This level of control tends to appeal most to:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Experienced Investors:</strong> People who have a solid grasp of financial markets and want to take a hands-on approach to building their portfolio.</li>
<li><strong>Small Business Owners:</strong> Entrepreneurs who might want to use their super to purchase their own business premises—a strategy unique to SMSFs.</li>
<li><strong>Families:</strong> Relatives looking to pool their superannuation to access larger investment opportunities, like a significant property purchase, and manage their retirement strategy as a group.</li>
</ul>
<p>Ultimately, setting up an SMSF is about making a conscious decision to move from being a passive saver to an active architect of your own wealth.</p>
<h2>How an SMSF Works in The Real World</h2>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdn.outrank.so/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/46260c68-a965-48fd-bf78-10815be7954c/what-is-a-self-managed-super-fund-smsf-purchase.jpg" alt="A smiling man presents keys and an &#039;SMSF purchase&#039; document to another man." /></figure></p>
<p>It’s one thing to understand the concept of an SMSF, but seeing how it actually operates day-to-day is another story. At its core, a self managed super fund is a private trust where the members are also the trustees. This legal structure is the engine room of your fund, and getting it started involves a few foundational, non-negotiable steps.</p>
<p>Every SMSF is built upon a legally binding <strong>trust deed</strong>. Think of this document as the constitution for your fund—it lays out all the rules for how it will be established, operated, and eventually wound up. Once the trust deed is in place, you have to set up a dedicated bank account used only for the fund’s transactions.</p>
<p>Crucially, every asset the SMSF owns must be held in the name of the trustees <em>on behalf of the fund</em>. This creates a crystal-clear legal separation between your personal finances and your retirement savings, which is a cornerstone of SMSF compliance. This separation ensures the fund&#039;s assets are protected and managed for their one true purpose: providing for your retirement.</p>
<h3>Crafting Your Investment Blueprint</h3>
<p>While the trust deed provides the rules, the <strong>investment strategy</strong> provides the roadmap. This is a mandatory written plan that details your fund&#039;s investment objectives and the specific methods you&#039;ll use to achieve them. It’s not a &quot;set and forget&quot; document, either—it has to be reviewed regularly and must consider the circumstances of all members, including their age and risk tolerance.</p>
<p>Your strategy needs to be specific enough to guide your decisions but flexible enough to adapt to changing market conditions. It&#039;s the document you&#039;ll refer back to every time you consider buying or selling an asset, ensuring every decision is purposeful and aligned with your long-term goals. To really understand how an SMSF functions, you need to grasp how to structure and manage the investments it holds, including how to <a href="https://finzer.io/en/blog/how-to-build-a-stock-portfolio">build an investment portfolio</a> that works for your unique situation.</p>
<h3>A Real World Example of an SMSF in Action</h3>
<p>Let&#039;s make this tangible with a practical scenario. Picture Chloe, a Melbourne-based entrepreneur who runs a successful graphic design agency. For years, she’s been renting a commercial studio, watching her rent payments disappear into her landlord&#039;s pocket.</p>
<p>Chloe decides to set up an SMSF with her partner. After getting professional advice, they establish a trust deed, register their fund with the ATO, and roll over their existing super balances into a new SMSF bank account. They also create a detailed investment strategy that includes purchasing commercial property.</p>
<p>Using the funds now in their SMSF, combined with a compliant borrowing arrangement, they buy the very same studio Chloe has been renting.</p>
<p>Here’s how this single move benefits them:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Rent becomes an investment:</strong> The rent Chloe&#039;s business pays now goes directly into her <em>own</em> SMSF. It’s a tax-deductible business expense that simultaneously builds her retirement savings.</li>
<li><strong>Asset security:</strong> The business has a secure, long-term home, free from the whims of a landlord.</li>
<li><strong>Capital growth:</strong> Any increase in the property&#039;s value directly benefits their super fund, growing their retirement nest egg.</li>
</ul>
<p>This is a prime example of an SMSF at its most powerful—a vehicle for strategic wealth creation that can align with both your business and personal financial goals. It&#039;s a strategy that&#039;s becoming incredibly popular among savvy Australian investors.</p>
<p>The data paints a clear picture. As of June 2025, there are over <strong>653,000</strong> funds with <strong>1.2 million</strong> members, holding assets that surged to <strong>$1,073.4 billion</strong> by September 2025. This reflects a <strong>4.8%</strong> year-on-year growth and shows that SMSFs are a significant force, making up a huge portion of Australia&#039;s total <strong>$4.5 trillion</strong> superannuation pool. You can discover more insights about these SMSF statistics directly from the ATO.</p>
<h2>Understanding Your Responsibilities as an SMSF Trustee</h2>
<iframe width="100%" style="aspect-ratio: 16 / 9" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/7Xlqswvf8pE" frameborder="0" allow="autoplay; encrypted-media" allowfullscreen></iframe>

<p>When you decide to set up a self managed super fund, you&#039;re not just becoming an investor—you’re stepping into the formal role of a <strong>trustee</strong>. This is a serious legal position that comes with a strict set of duties enforced by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO). Getting your head around these responsibilities isn&#039;t just a suggestion; it’s the absolute foundation of running a compliant and successful SMSF.</p>
<p>Your number one job, above everything else, is to act in the best financial interests of all the fund&#039;s members. Every single decision, from the investment strategy you map out to the specific assets you buy, must be made for the <strong>sole purpose</strong> of providing retirement benefits. This is known as the &#039;<strong>sole purpose test</strong>&#039;, and it’s the golden rule that guides everything you do as a trustee.</p>
<p>Managing an SMSF is so much more than just picking a few stocks or properties. It’s about being diligent with administration, sticking to the rules, and committing to uphold the law. Dropping the ball here can lead to some pretty hefty penalties, so it&#039;s vital to know exactly what’s expected of you from day one.</p>
<h3>The Core Duties of an SMSF Trustee</h3>
<p>As a trustee, you are personally on the hook for the fund&#039;s actions. The ATO lays out several non-negotiable responsibilities that you must tick off each year to keep your fund compliant. Think of these tasks as the operational engine of your SMSF.</p>
<p>Here’s a rundown of the key duties you&#039;ll need to manage:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Investment Strategy:</strong> You must create, follow, and regularly review a written investment strategy for your fund. This isn&#039;t just a document to file away; it needs to genuinely consider the personal circumstances of all members, like their age, appetite for risk, and retirement goals. It also has to address diversification and ensure the fund has enough cash to pay benefits when needed.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Valuation of Assets:</strong> Every asset in the fund must be valued at its current market value each year. This is absolutely critical for preparing accurate financial accounts and member statements.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Accepting Contributions:</strong> You need to make sure that any contributions coming into the fund are compliant with super laws and the fund&#039;s own trust deed.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Paying Benefits:</strong> When a member becomes eligible to access their super, you are responsible for paying out their benefits—either as a lump sum or a pension—in line with the law and the trust deed.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p>These tasks require your ongoing attention and a proactive approach. They aren&#039;t &#039;set and forget&#039; jobs but a continuous cycle of review and action throughout the financial year. To learn more about optimising your financial position, check out our guide on <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/how-to-reduce-taxable-income/">how to reduce taxable income in Australia</a>.</p>
<h3>Record-Keeping and Reporting Obligations</h3>
<p>Meticulous record-keeping is easily one of the most critical parts of being an SMSF trustee. The ATO can ask to see your records at any time, and they expect them to be accurate, organised, and complete. In fact, messy paperwork is one of the most common reasons SMSFs get into trouble.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>&quot;Being an SMSF trustee means you are the fund’s chief administrator. The buck stops with you. Proper record-keeping isn&#039;t just good practice; it&#039;s a legal requirement that protects the fund, its members, and you from ATO penalties.&quot;</p>
</blockquote>
<p>You’ll need to hang on to detailed records for different periods:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Five Years:</strong> Keep minutes of trustee meetings, records of any changes to who the trustees are, and copies of all reports you give to members.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Ten Years:</strong> Retain accounting records that show the fund&#039;s financial transactions and position, as well as the annual financial statements.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p>Beyond just keeping records, you have annual reporting duties. Every year, you have to arrange for an independent, ATO-approved auditor to go over your fund. This auditor will check your fund&#039;s financial statements and make sure you’re complying with super laws. After the audit is done, you’re required to lodge an SMSF annual return with the ATO.</p>
<p>This combination of diligent record-keeping, independent auditing, and annual reporting ensures everything is transparent and accountable. It proves to the regulators that your fund is being managed correctly. Juggling these compliance deadlines can be demanding, which is why many trustees lean on professional support from firms like Trew North Accounting to stay on track and avoid the stress of trying to manage it all alone.</p>
<h2>Is an SMSF The Right Choice for You?</h2>
<p>Deciding to start a self managed super fund is a major financial crossroad. It’s a move that offers a level of control and flexibility you simply can’t get in a standard super fund, but this freedom comes hand-in-hand with some serious legal and administrative commitments. Making the right choice means honestly looking at not just your financial goals, but also your personality and whether you’re ready to take on a significant new responsibility.</p>
<p>Think of it this way: an SMSF isn&#039;t a passive investment. It&#039;s an active management role. It demands a hands-on approach, a solid grasp of investment principles, and the discipline to stay on top of a mountain of regulations. Before you even think about diving in, it&#039;s critical to weigh the powerful advantages against the considerable drawbacks to see if it truly fits your long-term vision for retirement.</p>
<h3>SMSF vs Retail and Industry Super Funds: A Quick Comparison</h3>
<p>When you stack an SMSF against a typical retail or industry fund, the differences are stark. One offers complete autonomy, while the other provides a professionally managed, set-and-forget experience. Getting your head around these core distinctions is the first step in figuring out which path is right for you.</p>
<p>Here’s a high-level comparison to make the key differences clear.</p>
<h4>Self Managed Super Fund (SMSF)</h4>
<ul>
<li><strong>Control Over Investments:</strong> You are the investment manager. You can invest directly in shares, property, term deposits, and more, all guided by your unique strategy.</li>
<li><strong>Flexibility &amp; Strategy:</strong> High. Allows for sophisticated tax strategies, especially in retirement. You can also pool funds with up to five other members for larger investments.</li>
<li><strong>Responsibility:</strong> The buck stops with you. You&#039;re personally responsible for all investment decisions, admin, record-keeping, and legal compliance.</li>
<li><strong>Costs &amp; Fees:</strong> Generally fixed annual costs (ATO levy, audit, accounting fees). Can be more cost-effective for larger balances.</li>
<li><strong>Time Commitment:</strong> Significant and ongoing. It’s like running a small business dedicated to your retirement.</li>
<li><strong>Legal Protections:</strong> You have <strong>no access</strong> to the government’s statutory compensation scheme for losses due to fraud or theft.</li>
</ul>
<h4>Retail/Industry Super Fund</h4>
<ul>
<li><strong>Control Over Investments:</strong> Your choices are limited to a pre-selected menu of investment options (e.g., Conservative, Balanced, High Growth). You don&#039;t control the specific assets.</li>
<li><strong>Flexibility &amp; Strategy:</strong> Low. Strategic options are generally limited to switching between the fund&#039;s set investment choices. Tax strategies are fund-wide, not personal.</li>
<li><strong>Responsibility:</strong> Minimal. A professional trustee manages the fund on your behalf. Your main job is to check your statements.</li>
<li><strong>Costs &amp; Fees:</strong> Typically percentage-based fees that grow with your balance, plus other potential admin or investment fees.</li>
<li><strong>Time Commitment:</strong> Very low. The fund&#039;s professionals do all the heavy lifting for you.</li>
<li><strong>Legal Protections:</strong> Members are covered by the government compensation scheme, offering a safety net against fraudulent activity.</li>
</ul>
<p>Ultimately, the choice comes down to what you value more: the total control and strategic potential of an SMSF, or the simplicity and professional oversight of a traditional fund.</p>
<h3>The Power of Control and Flexibility</h3>
<p>So, what’s the big deal about running your own super fund? The primary drawcard is unparalleled control. You get to build a portfolio from the ground up that perfectly reflects your risk appetite and retirement goals. No more being shoehorned into a one-size-fits-all investment option.</p>
<p>For business owners, this can be a game-changer. The ability to use your super to buy your own commercial premises can turn rent payments into retirement contributions. This level of strategic customisation is one of the key <a href="https://everglow.au/advantages-of-self-managed-super-funds/">advantages of Self Managed Super Funds</a>.</p>
<p>This appeal is reflected in the massive uptake of SMSFs across Australia. By <strong>September 2025</strong>, self-managed super funds numbered exactly <strong>661,384</strong> across the country, holding a staggering <strong>1.22 million</strong> members. This isn&#039;t just a niche trend; it&#039;s a seismic shift in how Aussies are securing their future.</p>
<p>Total SMSF assets have smashed through the <strong>$1 trillion</strong> barrier to reach <strong>$1.07 trillion</strong>. That&#039;s a whopping <strong>25%</strong> of Australia&#039;s entire superannuation pool, proving SMSFs are a powerhouse for serious investors.</p>
<h3>What’s the Magic Number to Start an SMSF?</h3>
<p>One of the most critical questions to ask is whether your super balance is large enough to make an SMSF worthwhile. While there’s no legally mandated minimum, the general consensus among financial experts is that the fixed running costs make them less economical for smaller balances.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>A common rule of thumb suggests that a starting balance of at least <strong>$200,000</strong> is needed for an SMSF to begin being cost-effective compared to traditional funds. Many advisors recommend a balance closer to <strong>$500,000</strong> to truly maximise the benefits.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Why this figure? The annual costs of running an SMSF—including the ATO levy, audit fees, and administration—can easily amount to a few thousand dollars per year. If these fixed costs represent a high percentage of your total fund balance, they can seriously eat into your investment returns, defeating the purpose of running your own fund.</p>
<p>As your balance grows, however, these fixed costs become a smaller and smaller fraction of your assets, making the structure far more efficient.</p>
<h2>Essential Steps to Set Up Your SMSF</h2>
<p>So, you’ve weighed up the pros and cons and decided the control and flexibility of a self managed super fund is the right move for you. Fantastic. The next part is the setup process, and getting this right from day one is absolutely critical.</p>
<p>Think of it like laying the foundations for a house. If the slab isn’t perfectly level and square, you’ll be dealing with the consequences for years. Getting these foundational steps right prevents a world of future headaches and sets your fund up for long-term success. The setup isn’t a single action; it’s a series of deliberate, legally required steps that build on each other to create the structure that will protect your retirement savings.</p>
<p>This decision tree visualises the core choice you make when opting for an SMSF: embracing greater control over your investments while accepting full responsibility for managing them.</p>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdn.outrank.so/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/a17d64c6-c57e-4f3e-ac6c-4034417ce40c/what-is-a-self-managed-super-fund-smsf-choice.jpg" alt="Flowchart illustrating the decision path for choosing a Self-Managed Super Fund (SMSF) based on control and responsibility." /></figure></p>
<p>As the infographic shows, the path to an SMSF is a balance between the appeal of direct investment control and the commitment to rigorous trustee duties.</p>
<h3>Step 1: Choose Your Members and Trustee Structure</h3>
<p>First things first, you need to decide who will be in the fund with you. An SMSF can have between <strong>one and six members</strong>. The golden rule is that every member must also be a trustee, making everyone equally responsible for the fund’s decisions and compliance.</p>
<p>Next, you have to choose a trustee structure. This is a huge decision with long-term consequences for how your fund is administered and how its assets are owned.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Individual Trustees:</strong> All members of the fund are simply appointed as individual trustees. This is often quicker to set up initially, but it can get messy down the track. When members join or leave the fund, the legal title for every single asset has to be updated, which can be a real pain.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Corporate Trustee:</strong> A proprietary limited (Pty Ltd) company is set up to act as the trustee for the fund, and all the members are directors of that company. While it means setting up a company first, this structure provides a crystal-clear separation of assets and makes administrative changes—like adding a new member—infinitely simpler.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>Step 2: Appoint Professionals and Create the Trust Deed</h3>
<p>While you are the trustee, you absolutely do not have to go it alone. In fact, you shouldn’t. Appointing professionals like an accountant who specialises in SMSFs and an independent auditor isn&#039;t just a smart move; it&#039;s a practical necessity. These experts will be your guide on compliance, help with the administration, and perform the legally required annual audit. To see how we can help, you can learn more about our dedicated <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/services/self-managed-super-funds/">self managed super fund services</a>.</p>
<p>With your professional team in place, you’ll then create the fund&#039;s <strong>trust deed</strong>. This is the single most important legal document for your SMSF—it’s the rulebook. It must be prepared by a legal professional to ensure it’s tailored to your needs while still complying with all superannuation laws.</p>
<h3>Step 3: Register the Fund and Open a Bank Account</h3>
<p>Once the trust is legally established, it’s time to make it official with the Australian Taxation Office (ATO). This involves applying for an Australian Business Number (ABN) and a Tax File Number (TFN) specifically for the fund. Once the ATO gives you the green light, your SMSF officially becomes a regulated superannuation fund.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>The moment your SMSF is registered, it becomes a distinct legal entity. This is why the next step—opening a separate bank account—is non-negotiable for maintaining the strict separation of fund assets from personal finances.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>You must open a dedicated bank account in the name of the fund&#039;s trustee(s). Every cent—contributions, rollovers, investment income, and expenses—must flow through this account. Using a personal bank account for SMSF transactions is a serious breach of the rules and will land you in hot water with the ATO.</p>
<h3>Step 4: Roll Over Existing Super Balances</h3>
<p>The final major step is to move your super from your existing retail or industry funds into your new SMSF bank account. This is called a rollover. You’ll need to give your old funds the ABN and other details of your newly registered SMSF to get the ball rolling.</p>
<p>Once the money lands in your SMSF bank account, you are officially at the helm. From this point on, you can start executing your investment strategy and actively managing your retirement nest egg, all within the rules set out in your trust deed and Australian super law.</p>
<h2>Common Questions About Self Managed Super Funds</h2>
<p>Venturing into the world of self managed super funds always brings up a few practical questions about what you can and can’t do. Getting clear, straightforward answers is vital for staying on the right side of the law and making smart decisions for your retirement.</p>
<p>Below, we tackle some of the most common queries we hear from trustees. Understanding these rules helps clarify what an SMSF is and why it has to operate within such strict legal boundaries. It’s not just about investment freedom; it’s about compliant, responsible management.</p>
<h3>Can I Use My SMSF to Buy a House to Live In?</h3>
<p>The answer to this one is a hard and fast <strong>no</strong>. A core principle of superannuation law, known as the &#039;sole purpose test&#039;, is crystal clear: your super fund must be maintained <em>exclusively</em> to provide retirement benefits for its members.</p>
<p>Using your SMSF to buy a property for your personal use, or for any member or their relatives to live in, is a serious breach of this rule. The ATO doesn&#039;t take this lightly and imposes severe penalties for violations.</p>
<p>However, your SMSF <em>can</em> purchase an investment property (either residential or commercial), as long as it&#039;s leased to an unrelated party at a competitive, market-based rate.</p>
<h3>How Much Does It Cost to Run an SMSF?</h3>
<p>While the exact costs can vary, you should budget for both one-off setup fees and ongoing annual expenses. These yearly costs are essential for keeping your fund compliant and running smoothly.</p>
<p>Annual expenses typically include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>ATO Supervisory Levy:</strong> A fee paid directly to the Australian Taxation Office.</li>
<li><strong>Audit Fee:</strong> Payment to an independent, approved SMSF auditor who checks your fund&#039;s compliance.</li>
<li><strong>Administration Fees:</strong> Costs for accounting, tax lodgements, and general fund management.</li>
</ul>
<p>These annual costs can range from <strong>$2,000 to over $5,000</strong>, depending on how complex your investments are. This is why SMSFs generally become more cost-effective once the fund balance climbs above <strong>$200,000</strong>, as these fixed costs then represent a smaller percentage of your total assets.</p>
<p>You can find more detailed answers to your questions on our comprehensive <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/faqs/">SMSF FAQs page</a>.</p>
<h3>What Happens If a Member Passes Away?</h3>
<p>When a member dies, their superannuation balance must be paid out as a death benefit. The fund’s trustees are legally required to follow the instructions laid out in the SMSF&#039;s trust deed.</p>
<p>If the deceased member made a valid <strong>binding death benefit nomination (BDBN)</strong>, the trustees have no choice but to pay the benefit to the nominated beneficiaries. This is typically paid to their dependents or their legal estate. This process involves complex legal and tax implications, making professional guidance absolutely essential to ensure it&#039;s handled correctly and sensitively.</p>
<hr>
<p>Navigating the rules of your SMSF can feel demanding, but you don&#039;t have to do it alone. The expert team at <strong>Trew North Accounting</strong> provides clear, practical guidance to help you manage your fund with confidence and stay compliant. <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au">Contact us today</a> to learn how we can support your retirement goals.</p>

		<title><![CDATA[Self Managed Super Fund Costs: self managed super fund costs explained]]></title>
		<link>https://tnaccounting.com.au/?p=14626</link>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://tnaccounting.com.au/?p=14626</guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Thinking about starting a Self-Managed Super Fund (SMSF)? It&#039;s a big step, giving you direct control over your retirement savings. But before you jump in, it’s absolutely vital to get your head around the full picture of <strong>self managed super fund costs</strong>.</p>
<p>Unlike your standard industry or retail fund that slices off a percentage of your balance each year, an SMSF operates on a different model. It often involves a series of fixed costs for setup, admin, and compliance.</p>
<p>This structure can be incredibly cost-effective, especially for larger balances, but you need to know exactly what you’re signing up for.</p>
<h2>Understanding the True Cost of an SMSF</h2>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdn.outrank.so/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/c2c02ab7-cf4f-4e57-a634-9442d0ec9e7b/self-managed-super-fund-costs-cost-breakdown.jpg" alt="A document titled &#039;SMSF Costs&#039; with a pie chart, calculator, and pen on a wooden desk." /></figure></p>
<p>Before we dive into the nitty-gritty of SMSF expenses, it’s worth taking a step back. If you&#039;re still getting familiar with the basics, this overview of <a href="https://wealthcollective.co/what-is-superannuation-in-australia/">What Is Superannuation in Australia</a> is a great starting point.</p>
<p>Having that foundational knowledge is key to understanding how an SMSF fits into the broader retirement savings system.</p>
<p>Think of running an SMSF less like having a simple savings account and more like managing a small business—a business dedicated entirely to your retirement. The costs are transparent and predictable, but they fall into several distinct buckets that you need to be aware of.</p>
<h3>The Four Main Categories of SMSF Costs</h3>
<p>To get a clear picture of the financial commitment, it helps to break down the expenses into four key areas. This framework cuts through the common myth that SMSFs are outrageously expensive and gives you a solid foundation for budgeting.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>One-Off Establishment Fees:</strong> These are the initial, upfront costs to legally get your fund up and running, ready to accept contributions and start investing.</li>
<li><strong>Ongoing Annual Administration:</strong> This covers the recurring fees for the essential stuff—think accounting, lodging the tax return, and the mandatory independent audit.</li>
<li><strong>Mandatory Government Levies:</strong> Every SMSF has to pay a fixed supervisory levy to the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) each year. It’s non-negotiable.</li>
<li><strong>Variable Investment Costs:</strong> These expenses are tied directly to the assets you choose. This could be brokerage fees for buying shares, management fees for a managed fund, or property management costs.</li>
</ul>
<p>The big difference here compared to retail or industry funds is that many SMSF costs are <strong>fixed</strong>. This is a game-changer.</p>
<p>It means as your fund balance grows, the <em>relative</em> cost of running your SMSF can drop significantly, making it more efficient over time.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>The real power of an SMSF&#039;s cost structure is its transparency. You see exactly where every dollar is going, from accounting fees to brokerage. This gives you the control to optimise expenses and ultimately maximise your retirement nest egg.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Getting a handle on this structure is the first and most important step. It helps you make an informed decision about whether an SMSF truly aligns with your financial goals and, just as importantly, your willingness to take on a more hands-on role.</p>
<h2>Your Initial SMSF Setup and Establishment Fees</h2>
<p>Starting an SMSF isn&#039;t as simple as just opening a new bank account. Think of it like laying the foundations for a house—you need to get the structure right from the very beginning to avoid expensive problems down the track.</p>
<p>This initial phase involves a series of one-off establishment fees that create the legal and financial framework your fund needs to operate legally.</p>
<p>While it might be tempting to cut corners here, these setup fees are a critical investment. Paying for a professional setup ensures your fund ticks all the regulatory boxes from day one, giving you peace of mind and a solid base to build your retirement wealth.</p>
<p>Let&#039;s break down exactly what these upfront costs cover.</p>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdn.outrank.so/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/9842e943-bf01-4e4e-8452-42c09d700d28/self-managed-super-fund-costs-trust-fund.jpg" alt="A desk with a laptop, a &#039;Trust Deed&#039; folder, &#039;Fund Account&#039; documents, and a credit card, representing financial planning." /></figure></p>
<h3>Core Establishment Costs Explained</h3>
<p>To get your fund off the ground, you’ll need to budget for several key components. Each one plays a distinct and legally necessary role in forming your SMSF.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Trust Deed Creation:</strong> This is the legal rulebook for your SMSF. A specialist lawyer or service provider drafts this document, which outlines how the fund will be established, managed, and eventually wound up. A well-drafted deed is crucial for compliance and typically costs between <strong>$200 and $700</strong>.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Fund and ABN Registration:</strong> Your SMSF must be registered with the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) and have its own Australian Business Number (ABN). This officially recognises it as a superannuation entity. This registration process is usually bundled into a provider&#039;s setup package.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Corporate Trustee Setup:</strong> While you <em>can</em> have individual trustees, establishing a company to act as the trustee is highly recommended. This structure provides far better asset protection and makes administrative tasks like adding or removing members much simpler. The ASIC registration fee for a proprietary company is a key part of this cost, which can range from <strong>$700 to $1,500</strong>.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>Setting Up Your Financials</h3>
<p>Once the legal structure is in place, your fund needs its own financial identity. This means setting up dedicated accounts to keep its assets completely separate from your personal finances—a non-negotiable rule.</p>
<p>A dedicated bank account is mandatory for an SMSF. All contributions, investment income, and expenses must flow through this account to maintain a clear audit trail for the ATO.</p>
<p>Some banks offer specialised SMSF accounts with no monthly fees, while others might have charges, so it definitely pays to compare your options.</p>
<p>Understanding the scale of the SMSF sector can provide valuable context. By 2024, total expenses across Australia&#039;s SMSFs reached a staggering <strong>$11.2 billion</strong>, with administration and operating costs making up a huge chunk of that.</p>
<p>This growth highlights just how many Aussies are demanding more control and flexibility, especially business owners wanting to invest in assets like commercial property.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Establishing your SMSF with a solid legal and financial foundation is not just a regulatory hurdle—it&#039;s the most important step in protecting your retirement assets and ensuring smooth, long-term fund management.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>By budgeting for these one-time fees, you&#039;re positioning your fund for success. For personalised guidance on navigating the setup process, you might be interested in our expert <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/services/self-managed-super-funds/">self-managed super funds services</a>.</p>
<p>Getting it right from the start will save you time, money, and a lot of stress in the long run.</p>
<h2>Breaking Down Ongoing Annual Administration Costs</h2>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdn.outrank.so/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/5d000443-b267-4ebe-a979-323bd18aa0e4/self-managed-super-fund-costs-smsf-audit.jpg" alt="A desk with an &#039;Annual SMSF Audit&#039; document, a calendar marking &#039;ATO levy&#039;, a pen, and eyeglasses." /></figure></p>
<p>Once your SMSF is up and running, the focus shifts from one-off setup fees to the recurring annual costs. Think of these ongoing administration expenses as the engine room of your SMSF—they cover all the essential compliance and reporting tasks needed to keep your fund in good standing with the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).</p>
<p>Getting a handle on these yearly fees is critical for figuring out if an SMSF is truly affordable for you in the long run. While they’re generally predictable, they are made up of several distinct parts, each playing a vital role in keeping your fund on track.</p>
<h3>Core Annual Compliance Fees</h3>
<p>Every single year, your SMSF has to meet specific reporting obligations. No exceptions.</p>
<p>These aren&#039;t tasks you can afford to get wrong, which is why they require professional expertise and form the bedrock of your annual <strong>self managed super fund costs</strong>.</p>
<p>Let&#039;s unpack the main expenses you can expect to pay each year.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Accounting and Financial Statements:</strong> This is where your fund&#039;s annual financial reports are prepared, including statements of financial position and operations. Good accounting is the foundation for everything else, typically costing between <strong>$1,000 and $3,000</strong>, depending on how complex your investments are.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>SMSF Annual Return (SAR) Lodgement:</strong> Your fund has to lodge a specialised tax return with the ATO each year. It reports the fund’s income, member contributions, and tax liabilities. This service is almost always bundled in with the accounting fees.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Independent Audit:</strong> It&#039;s required by law. An independent, ASIC-registered auditor must review your fund&#039;s finances and compliance annually. This audit is your proof that you&#039;ve followed superannuation laws. For a straightforward fund, expect audit fees to range from <strong>$350 to $700</strong>.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>The Mandatory ATO Supervisory Levy</h3>
<p>On top of the professional service fees, every SMSF has to pay a fixed government charge.</p>
<p>The <strong>ATO Supervisory Levy</strong> is a non-negotiable fee that helps cover the cost of the ATO&#039;s regulatory oversight of the entire SMSF sector. It’s currently set at <strong>$259 per year</strong>.</p>
<p>It&#039;s important to know this levy is collected in arrears when you lodge your first annual return and for every year after that.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>The annual audit is not just a box-ticking exercise. It&#039;s a critical safeguard that protects the integrity of your fund and ensures you are meeting your duties as a trustee, preventing potentially severe ATO penalties.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>This blend of accounting, tax, audit, and the ATO levy makes up the core of your predictable annual costs. However, <em>how</em> these services are delivered can massively impact your total bill.</p>
<p>Keeping meticulous records throughout the year is one of the best ways to keep professional fees down. This is why many trustees lean on expert support; you can learn more about our streamlined <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/services/bookkeeping/">bookkeeping services for small businesses</a> and SMSFs if you need a hand.</p>
<h3>Comparing Administration Service Models</h3>
<p>Not all SMSF administration services are the same. You&#039;ll find a whole spectrum of options out there, from completely hands-off solutions to DIY platforms where you do most of the heavy lifting.</p>
<p>The right choice comes down to your budget, how much time you&#039;re willing to commit, and your comfort level with handling compliance risks.</p>
<p>To help you decide, let&#039;s look at the different types of ongoing costs and services you&#039;ll encounter.</p>
<h4>Typical Annual SMSF Administration Costs Breakdown</h4>
<p>This section breaks down the common ongoing fees so you can see what to expect each year.</p>
<h5>Accounting &amp; Tax Return</h5>
<ul>
<li><strong>Typical Cost:</strong> $1,000 - $3,000+ per year.</li>
<li><strong>Description:</strong> This covers the preparation of financial statements and lodgement of the SMSF Annual Return (SAR) with the ATO.</li>
</ul>
<h5>Independent Audit</h5>
<ul>
<li><strong>Typical Cost:</strong> $350 - $700 per year.</li>
<li><strong>Description:</strong> A mandatory annual audit by an ASIC-registered auditor to verify compliance with superannuation laws.</li>
</ul>
<h5>ATO Supervisory Levy</h5>
<ul>
<li><strong>Typical Cost:</strong> $259 (fixed) per year.</li>
<li><strong>Description:</strong> A non-negotiable government fee charged to every SMSF to fund regulatory oversight.</li>
</ul>
<h5>Administration Platform Fee</h5>
<ul>
<li><strong>Typical Cost:</strong> $200 - $1,500 per year.</li>
<li><strong>Description:</strong> Fees for software or platforms that help automate data feeds and record-keeping, if you choose to use one.</li>
</ul>
<h5>Total Estimated Core Cost</h5>
<ul>
<li><strong>Typical Cost:</strong> $1,809 - $5,459+ per year.</li>
<li><strong>Description:</strong> This represents the combined typical range for essential annual compliance and administration costs for an SMSF.</li>
</ul>
<p>These figures give you a solid baseline, but your final costs will depend on the service model you choose.</p>
<h3>Full-Service Administration</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>What it is:</strong> A comprehensive package where a provider, like an accountant or a specialist firm, handles everything. This includes daily transaction processing, financial reporting, lodging the tax return, and organising the audit.</li>
<li><strong>Best for:</strong> Trustees who want a &quot;set and forget&quot; solution. It’s ideal if you value expert support and prefer to focus on your investment strategy rather than paperwork.</li>
<li><strong>Typical Cost:</strong> Generally ranges from <strong>$2,000 to $5,000+</strong> per year.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Online or DIY Platforms</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>What it is:</strong> Software-based solutions that automate a lot of the data entry and reporting. You’re responsible for inputting or reconciling transactions, and the platform generates the reports needed for your tax return and audit.</li>
<li><strong>Best for:</strong> Cost-conscious, hands-on trustees who are confident managing their own record-keeping and just need the basic compliance framework.</li>
<li><strong>Typical Cost:</strong> Often lower, from <strong>$800 to $1,800</strong> per year, but watch out for extra charges for support or handling complex transactions.</li>
</ul>
<p>The key trade-off here is cost versus service. A full-service model provides a safety net and expert guidance, which can save you from making costly compliance mistakes.</p>
<p>A DIY platform lowers the direct fee but puts a much greater responsibility on your shoulders to get everything right. Carefully weighing this balance is essential when managing your overall <strong>self managed super fund costs</strong>.</p>
<h2>How Your Investments Impact Overall Fund Costs</h2>
<p>While setup and annual admin fees are fixed and predictable, they only tell half the story. The other big piece of the puzzle for your <strong>self managed super fund costs</strong> comes from variable expenses tied directly to your investment choices.</p>
<p>These are the costs that can quietly build up and start eating into your returns if you’re not watching them closely.</p>
<p>Unlike the fixed fees for compliance work, you are firmly in the driver’s seat here. The assets you choose, how often you trade, and whether you use leverage will directly shape how much you pay.</p>
<p>A smart investment strategy isn&#039;t just about picking winners; it’s also about cutting out unnecessary financial drag.</p>
<h3>Common Investment-Related Expenses</h3>
<p>As a trustee, you have the freedom to invest in a massive range of assets, from direct shares and property to managed funds. But each of these asset classes comes with its own cost structure, which you need to factor into both your budget and your performance calculations.</p>
<p>Here are the most common investment costs you&#039;ll run into.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Brokerage Fees:</strong> Every time you buy or sell assets like shares or Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) on the market, you&#039;ll pay a brokerage fee. These costs can vary wildly between platforms, from just a few dollars to a percentage of the trade value.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Management Expense Ratios (MERs):</strong> If you invest in ETFs or managed funds, a percentage of your investment is skimmed off each year to cover the fund manager&#039;s operational costs. This fee, the MER, is charged indirectly and can range from as low as <strong>0.05%</strong> for simple index funds to over <strong>2%</strong> for actively managed funds.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Direct Property Costs:</strong> Holding a physical property in your SMSF comes with some hefty ongoing expenses. Think council and water rates, landlord insurance, property management fees, and a fund set aside for repairs and maintenance.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>The Impact of Your Trading Strategy</h3>
<p>The single biggest factor driving your investment costs is your strategy. An active trading approach, where you’re frequently buying and selling assets, will rack up brokerage fees far more quickly than a passive, buy-and-hold strategy.</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>Active Trader Example:</strong><br>An SMSF trustee making <strong>20 trades a month</strong> at an average brokerage cost of <strong>$15 per trade</strong> would spend <strong>$3,600</strong> on brokerage alone in a single year.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>Passive Investor Example:</strong><br>A trustee with a buy-and-hold strategy making only <strong>four trades per year</strong> at the same <strong>$15</strong> brokerage fee would spend just <strong>$60</strong> annually.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>The difference is stark and highlights how your behaviour directly hits your fund&#039;s bottom line. The appeal of active trading can be strong, but you have to weigh the <em>potential</em> for higher returns against the <em>certainty</em> of higher costs.</p>
<p>Making sure your investment activity aligns with your budget is a key part of managing your fund responsibly.</p>
<h3>Costs Associated with Borrowing (LRBAs)</h3>
<p>For trustees looking to use leverage to buy assets like property, another layer of costs comes into play through a Limited Recourse Borrowing Arrangement (LRBA). While it can be a powerful strategy, it introduces several new expenses you can&#039;t ignore.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Establishment Fees:</strong> Lenders charge significant upfront fees to set up an LRBA, which can easily run into the thousands.</li>
<li><strong>Legal and Advice Fees:</strong> Setting up the required bare trust and ensuring the whole arrangement is compliant often requires legal and financial advice, adding to the initial cost.</li>
<li><strong>Ongoing Interest Costs:</strong> The interest paid on the loan is a direct cost to the fund, reducing the net return you see from the investment.</li>
</ul>
<p>When planning your SMSF contributions to service these debts or grow your portfolio, it&#039;s crucial to be aware of the <a href="https://www.baronaccounting.com/post/concessional-contributions-cap-2026-kr">concessional contributions cap</a> to ensure you remain compliant. An LRBA adds a lot of complexity and cost, so it’s essential to do the sums carefully before jumping in.</p>
<h2>Is an SMSF Cost-Effective for You?</h2>
<p>This brings us to the million-dollar question—or perhaps the several-hundred-thousand-dollar question: how much money do you actually need for the typical <strong>self managed super fund costs</strong> to make financial sense?</p>
<p>Let&#039;s move past the guesswork. The answer is all about finding the breakeven point where running an SMSF becomes cheaper than staying in a standard retail or industry fund.</p>
<p>The fundamental difference lies in the fee structure. Most big super funds charge percentage-based fees that scale up as your balance grows. SMSFs, on the other hand, usually come with fixed administration costs. This creates a tipping point where taking control becomes the more economical choice.</p>
<h3>The Breakeven Point Explained</h3>
<p>Think of it like choosing a phone plan. A pay-as-you-go option is great if you barely make any calls, but for someone who&#039;s always on the phone, a fixed monthly plan is a no-brainer. Super funds work on the same logic.</p>
<p>When your super balance is on the smaller side, the percentage-based fees of an industry fund are often less than the fixed annual costs of running an SMSF.</p>
<p>But as your balance grows, that percentage fee starts to represent a much larger dollar figure, eventually overtaking the predictable, flat fees of an SMSF. That crossover point is your breakeven.</p>
<h3>Worked Example Scenario One: A $200,000 Balance</h3>
<p>Let’s put some numbers to it with a straightforward comparison.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Industry Fund:</strong> With an average total fee of <strong>1.0%</strong> per year, the cost would be <strong>$2,000</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Self Managed Super Fund:</strong> Assuming a typical annual administration cost of <strong>$3,500</strong>, the SMSF is <strong>$1,500 more expensive</strong> at this balance.</li>
</ul>
<p>In this scenario, sticking with the industry fund is clearly the cheaper option if we&#039;re only looking at fees.</p>
<h3>Worked Example Scenario Two: A $600,000 Balance</h3>
<p>Now, let&#039;s see what happens when the balance is larger, keeping the fee structures the same.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Industry Fund:</strong> That <strong>1.0%</strong> fee now adds up to a hefty <strong>$6,000</strong> per year.</li>
<li><strong>Self Managed Super Fund:</strong> The annual administration cost stays locked in at <strong>$3,500</strong>.</li>
</ul>
<p>At this level, the SMSF is suddenly <strong>$2,500 cheaper</strong> every single year. The fixed-cost model has become the more efficient path, and this saving will only get bigger as the fund balance continues to grow.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>The breakeven point isn&#039;t just a number; it&#039;s the moment your super balance becomes large enough to benefit from the economies of scale offered by an SMSF&#039;s fixed-fee structure. For many, this occurs when their balance is between <strong>$250,000 and $500,000</strong>.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>But remember, the decision isn&#039;t purely about the numbers. It also comes down to how much you value greater investment control, flexibility, and transparency over your retirement savings.</p>
<p>This flowchart shows the main areas where your investment choices will generate variable costs in an SMSF.</p>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdn.outrank.so/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/a3c7f62c-6c1a-480b-be6e-88cf73f696be/self-managed-super-fund-costs-smsf-costs.jpg" alt="Flowchart illustrating SMSF investment costs, showing average annual percentages for brokerage, property, and management fees." /></figure></p>
<p>The key takeaway here is that active trading (brokerage), property ownership, and investing in managed funds all add layers of cost that you, as the trustee, have direct control over.</p>
<h3>Understanding the Official Cost Data</h3>
<p>To make a fully informed decision, it pays to look at the real-world data. According to Australian Taxation Office (ATO) figures for the 2022/23 financial year, the median operating costs for SMSFs were <strong>$4,309</strong>. However, the average costs were significantly higher at <strong>$8,931</strong>.</p>
<p>This gap tells a story: while many funds operate very efficiently, a smaller number with complex structures or high-maintenance investments can face much steeper expenses.</p>
<p>For Melbourne-based business owners, partnering with an experienced firm that offers flat-rate pricing can keep these costs predictable and affordable, ensuring there are no nasty surprises. You can <a href="https://smsfaustralia.com.au/smsf-fee-comparisons/">discover more insights about SMSF fee comparisons on smsfaustralia.com.au</a>.</p>
<p>Ultimately, figuring out if an SMSF is cost-effective for you requires a personal calculation. You need to weigh the fixed annual fees against what you are currently paying in percentage-based fees, while also factoring in the value you place on having complete control over your investment strategy.</p>
<h2>Your Top SMSF Cost Questions Answered</h2>
<p>Let&#039;s wrap things up by tackling some of the most common questions trustees ask about managing <strong>self managed super fund costs</strong>. This is your quick-fire guide to the practical side of running your fund, designed to give you more confidence.</p>
<h3>Are Financial Advice Fees Tax-Deductible?</h3>
<p>Yes, but it’s not a simple blanket rule. Whether you can claim advice fees really hinges on <em>what</em> the advice was actually for.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Deductible Advice:</strong> Fees for advice that helps your fund generate assessable income are generally tax-deductible. Think ongoing investment strategy reviews or recommendations on specific assets.</li>
<li><strong>Non-Deductible Advice:</strong> Anything related to setting up the fund for the first time is usually considered a capital expense and can&#039;t be claimed. This includes initial advice on whether to start an SMSF or creating your very first investment strategy.</li>
</ul>
<h3>How Can I Reduce My Annual Audit Fee?</h3>
<p>Want to keep your audit fee down? It all comes down to being organised. An auditor’s time is literally money, so the less they have to spend chasing paperwork or untangling messy records, the less you&#039;ll pay. Simple as that.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Keep Impeccable Records:</strong> Log every single transaction with its supporting document—invoices, bank statements, and investment paperwork.</li>
<li><strong>Use Good Accounting Software:</strong> Modern cloud accounting platforms with bank feeds do most of the heavy lifting for you. They hand over a clean, organised set of books to your auditor, which saves a ton of time.</li>
<li><strong>Be Quick to Respond:</strong> If your auditor has questions, get back to them promptly and with all the information they need. Delays and back-and-forth communication can add to your final bill.</li>
</ul>
<h3>What Happens If I Pay the ATO Supervisory Levy Late?</h3>
<p>The ATO Supervisory Levy is due when you lodge your SMSF annual return. Paying it late is not a great idea, as it can attract penalties.</p>
<p>The ATO can hit you with a &#039;failure to lodge on time&#039; penalty, which can be pretty significant. It is absolutely critical to meet your lodgement deadlines to avoid these extra costs and keep your fund in good standing with the tax office.</p>
<p>For more in-depth answers, feel free to explore our full list of <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/faqs/">SMSF FAQs</a> for extra guidance.</p>

		<title><![CDATA[A Trustee's Guide to Self Managed Super Fund Advice]]></title>
