		<title><![CDATA[What Is a Chart of Accounts a Simple Guide for Your Business]]></title>
		<link>https://tnaccounting.com.au/?p=14850</link>
		<pubDate></pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[xdilvx]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://tnaccounting.com.au/?p=14850</guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Think of your business&#039;s finances. If they were a library, how would you find anything? You wouldn&#039;t just dump all the books in a pile on the floor. You&#039;d need a cataloguing system. A way to organise every book so you can find exactly what you need, when you need it.</p>
<p>That&#039;s precisely what a <strong>chart of accounts (COA)</strong> does for your money. It’s the central filing system for your business finances. It&#039;s a structured map that gives every dollar you earn, spend, own, or owe its own specific place. It’s not just a list of transactions. It’s the engine that powers your most critical financial reports, like the Profit and Loss statement and the Balance Sheet.</p>
<h2>Unlocking Your Business Finances with a Chart of Accounts</h2>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdnimg.co/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/8a7402bc-3ade-4fa2-bc1e-11654c044d38/what-is-a-chart-of-accounts-accounting-document.jpg" alt="A binder open to a &#039;Chart of Accounts&#039; page showing Assets, Liabilities, and Revenue categories, with a pen on a wooden table." /></figure></p>
<p>Let&#039;s stick with the library analogy. Your general ledger is the entire library collection. The chart of accounts is the Dewey Decimal System. It’s a complete, organised list that transforms a potentially messy pile of bank statements and receipts into a clear, logical map of all your financial activities.</p>
<p>To make this happen, every category is given a unique name and number. This includes everything from &#039;Office Supplies&#039; to &#039;Sales Revenue&#039;. This creates a consistent structure for recording every single transaction, which is the bedrock of accurate bookkeeping and smart financial management.</p>
<h3>The Purpose of a Chart of Accounts</h3>
<p>At its core, a chart of accounts brings order to financial chaos. It’s designed to let anyone quickly understand the flow of money in and out of the company. This includes you, your bookkeeper, or your accountant.</p>
<p>A well-designed COA helps you make smarter decisions on the fly. It helps you keep a finger on the pulse of your company&#039;s financial health. And it makes complying with accounting standards a whole lot simpler. It tells you <em>exactly</em> where your money is going and where it&#039;s coming from. No more guesswork.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>A chart of accounts is the foundational tool for financial visibility. Without it, generating accurate reports is nearly impossible. You are left to manually label transactions and guess about your business&#039;s performance.</p>
</blockquote>
<h3>Key Benefits for Small Businesses</h3>
<p>For a small business, a properly structured chart of accounts isn&#039;t just nice to have. It&#039;s invaluable. It&#039;s the backbone of your financial records. It ensures every dollar is tracked correctly for tax compliance and future growth planning.</p>
<p>Here’s why it’s so critical:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Improved Decision-Making:</strong> You can easily track specific expenses, see which revenue streams are performing best, and spot trends that inform your budget and strategy.</li>
<li><strong>Simplified Tax Time:</strong> When every transaction is already categorised correctly, preparing your Business Activity Statements (BAS) and end-of-year tax returns becomes a much smoother process.</li>
<li><strong>Accurate Financial Reporting:</strong> Generate reliable Profit &amp; Loss statements and Balance Sheets that give you a true, unvarnished picture of your business&#039;s financial position.</li>
<li><strong>Clear Budgeting and Forecasting:</strong> A huge benefit of a well-defined COA is the ability to clearly understand <a href="https://docparsemagic.com/blog/how-to-categorize-business-expenses">how to categorize business expenses</a>. This is absolutely crucial for creating a realistic budget and forecasting future performance.</li>
</ul>
<h2>The 5 Core Building Blocks of Your Finances</h2>
<p>Every chart of accounts, no matter how simple or complex, is built from just five fundamental types of accounts. Getting your head around these five core categories is the first real step to demystifying your business finances. It helps you take proper control of your books. Think of them as the main sections in your financial library. Each holds a specific kind of story about your business.</p>
<p>These five building blocks are <strong>Assets</strong>, <strong>Liabilities</strong>, <strong>Equity</strong>, <strong>Revenue</strong>, and <strong>Expenses</strong>. Together, they paint the complete picture of your company&#039;s financial health and performance. They give you the structure you need for accurate reports and, more importantly, smart decisions.</p>
<h3>Assets: What You Own</h3>
<p>Assets are all the valuable things your business owns that will provide some future economic benefit. This isn&#039;t just about the cash in your bank account. It covers everything you use to get the job done.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Cash in Bank:</strong> The most obvious one is the money sitting in your business bank accounts.</li>
<li><strong>Accounts Receivable:</strong> This is the money your customers owe you for products or services you’ve already delivered. It’s an asset because it’s cash that’s on its way to you.</li>
<li><strong>Inventory:</strong> The total value of all the products you have sitting on the shelf, ready to be sold.</li>
<li><strong>Equipment and Vehicles:</strong> Think computers, machinery, or the work ute. These are the physical tools that help you operate and generate income.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Liabilities: What You Owe</h3>
<p>Liabilities are the flip side of the coin. They represent all of your business&#039;s financial obligations. These are the debts you owe to other people and organisations. This is the money you&#039;re on the hook for, whether it’s to suppliers, the bank, or the tax office.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Accounts Payable:</strong> These are the bills you need to pay to your suppliers for goods or services you’ve already received.</li>
<li><strong>Credit Card Debt:</strong> The outstanding balance on your business credit cards.</li>
<li><strong>Business Loans:</strong> Money you’ve borrowed from a lender that needs to be paid back over time.</li>
<li><strong>GST Payable:</strong> The Goods and Services Tax you&#039;ve collected from your customers on behalf of the Australian Taxation Office (ATO). It was never really your money. You&#039;re just holding onto it before passing it on.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Equity: Your Business&#039;s Net Worth</h3>
<p>Equity can feel a bit abstract, but it’s actually quite simple. It’s what’s left over when you subtract all your liabilities from all your assets. In plain English, it represents the owner&#039;s (or owners&#039;) stake in the company.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Equity is what would be left for you if the business sold every single asset and paid off every single debt. It’s a measure of the investment and accumulated profits that truly belong to the owners.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>For a sole trader, this is often just called &#039;Owner&#039;s Equity&#039;. In a company structure, it gets a bit more complex. It includes funds from shareholders and <strong>retained earnings</strong>. These are simply the profits that have been ploughed back into the business instead of being paid out.</p>
<h3>Revenue: How You Make Money</h3>
<p>Revenue, also known as income, is all the money your business earns from its day-to-day operations. This is the &quot;top line&quot; on your Profit and Loss statement. It shows how much cash is flowing in before you account for any costs.</p>
<p>It’s always a good idea to split your revenue into different streams to see what’s working best. For instance, a local cafe might track:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Food Sales:</strong> Revenue from all the delicious menu items.</li>
<li><strong>Beverage Sales:</strong> Income specifically from coffee, tea, and cold drinks.</li>
<li><strong>Merchandise Sales:</strong> Money earned from selling things like branded keep-cups or bags of coffee beans.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Expenses: How You Spend Money</h3>
<p>Expenses are all the costs you incur to keep the lights on and generate that revenue. Tracking these meticulously is absolutely vital. It helps you understand your real profitability and keep your spending in check.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Operating Expenses:</strong> These are the day-to-day costs of doing business.</li>
<li><strong>Rent:</strong> Payments for your workshop, office, or retail space.</li>
<li><strong>Wages and Salaries:</strong> The money you pay your team.</li>
<li><strong>Marketing:</strong> All the costs associated with getting the word out about your business.</li>
<li><strong>Utilities:</strong> Your power, internet, and phone bills. The essentials that keep you connected.</li>
</ul>
<h2>How Account Numbering Creates Financial Clarity</h2>
<p>The numbers you see in a chart of accounts aren&#039;t just random digits. They&#039;re the secret sauce that organises your finances into a logical hierarchy. Think of this numbering system as a roadmap for your business&#039;s money. It makes it easy to see where every dollar is coming from and going to at a glance. It’s this structure that turns a long, jumbled list of accounts into a powerful framework for clear, reliable reporting.</p>
<p>At its core, the numbering system is all about grouping similar accounts. Each of the five main account types gets its own dedicated range of numbers. This ensures that when you pull up a financial report, related items are always clustered together. This gives you a consistent and coherent picture of your business&#039;s health.</p>
<p>This diagram shows how these five core financial blocks fit together in a standard hierarchy.</p>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdnimg.co/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/630e1297-7d61-4a71-a542-deb6bc8d88c5/what-is-a-chart-of-accounts-financial-hierarchy.jpg" alt="A financial hierarchy flowchart displays assets leading to liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses." /></figure></p>
<p>As you can see, the structure starts with <strong>Assets</strong> and <strong>Liabilities</strong>. These are the fundamental building blocks of your Balance Sheet.</p>
<h3>The Standard Numbering System</h3>
<p>Most businesses in Australia follow a pretty standard numbering sequence. It lines up perfectly with how financial statements are put together. Balance Sheet accounts (<strong>Assets</strong>, <strong>Liabilities</strong>, and <strong>Equity</strong>) are listed first. They are followed by the Profit and Loss accounts (<strong>Revenue</strong> and <strong>Expenses</strong>).</p>
<p>This consistency makes life so much easier. Everyone is speaking the same financial language. This includes you, your bookkeeper, or the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).</p>
<p>Here’s a typical breakdown of how it works:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>1000s for Assets:</strong> Accounts starting with a &#039;1&#039; represent everything your business owns. Common examples include <strong>1010</strong> for your primary bank account or <strong>1200</strong> for Accounts Receivable (money owed to you).</li>
<li><strong>2000s for Liabilities:</strong> Numbers beginning with a &#039;2&#039; show what you owe to others. You’ll often see <strong>2100</strong> for Accounts Payable (bills to pay) or <strong>2500</strong> for GST Payable.</li>
<li><strong>3000s for Equity:</strong> These accounts track the net worth of your business. Think <strong>3100</strong> for Owner&#039;s Capital or <strong>3200</strong> for Retained Earnings.</li>
<li><strong>4000s for Revenue:</strong> Your income streams all start with a &#039;4&#039;. For instance, <strong>4010</strong> might be for Consulting Services income, while <strong>4020</strong> is for Product Sales.</li>
<li><strong>5000s+ for Expenses:</strong> Every cost of running your business is grouped here, usually starting from &#039;5&#039; and going up. You might have <strong>6100</strong> for Rent or <strong>7100</strong> for Marketing.</li>
</ul>
<p>A chart of accounts essentially acts as a financial GPS for your business. It categorises every transaction into one of these codes. This system is absolutely vital for lodging your BAS accurately and getting through the end-of-financial-year madness without a headache.</p>
<h3>Why Gaps in the Numbers Are a Good Thing</h3>
<p>Ever noticed how accounts are often numbered with gaps in between, like <strong>1010</strong>, <strong>1020</strong>, then jumping to <strong>1050</strong>? That’s not an accident. It&#039;s smart planning.</p>
<p>Leaving intentional gaps in your numbering sequence gives you room to grow. It allows you to slot in new accounts down the track without having to completely reshuffle your entire chart.</p>
<p>As your business evolves, you might need to get more specific. Maybe you launch a new product or open a new savings account. If you’ve left those numerical gaps, you can simply add a new account right where it belongs. This keeps everything in perfect logical order. This kind of forward-thinking is a built-in feature of the <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/best-accounting-software-for-small-business-australia/">best accounting software for small businesses in Australia</a>. This ensures your financial system can scale right alongside your business.</p>
<h2>Real-World Chart of Accounts Examples</h2>
<p>Theory is one thing, but seeing a chart of accounts in action is where it all starts to click. Think of it less like a rigid, one-size-fits-all template. It is more like a flexible framework you mould to your specific business. How you make money, where you spend it, and what you own. That’s what your COA needs to reflect.</p>
<p>A well-crafted chart of accounts tells the unique financial story of your business. Let&#039;s walk through a few practical examples to show just how different the structures can be for different business models.</p>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdnimg.co/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/848fe0e6-4f5a-4fe5-a366-0fd46db8feb8/what-is-a-chart-of-accounts-business-concepts.jpg" alt="A wrench tagged &#039;Freelance&#039;, a retail bag tagged &#039;Retail&#039;, and a coffee cup for &#039;Consulting&#039; on a laptop." /></figure></p>
<h3>Example for a Freelance Contractor</h3>
<p>A freelance graphic designer or IT contractor typically has a pretty straightforward business model. Their chart of accounts will be simple and clean. It focuses on income from their services and the usual sole trader expenses. The goal here is clarity, not complexity.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Key Revenue Accounts:</strong> They might only need a single primary income account, like <strong>4010 - Design Services Revenue</strong>. If they occasionally run workshops, they could add <strong>4020 - Workshop &amp; Training Fees</strong> to track that income stream separately.</li>
<li><strong>Essential Expense Accounts:</strong> You’ll see the usual suspects here: <strong>6010 - Software Subscriptions</strong> (for things like Adobe Creative Cloud), <strong>6020 - Subcontractor Fees</strong> if they bring in other freelancers, and <strong>6030 - Home Office Expenses</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Balance Sheet Focus:</strong> Assets are usually minimal. A <strong>1010 - Business Cheque Account</strong> and <strong>1200 - Accounts Receivable</strong> to track unpaid invoices are often all that’s needed. On the other side, liabilities might just be a <strong>2100 - Business Credit Card</strong> and <strong>2500 - GST Payable</strong>.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Example for a Retail Store</h3>
<p>Now, let&#039;s switch gears to a retail business selling physical products. This is where things get more complex, especially when it comes to inventory. Their chart of accounts absolutely must track the cost of the goods they sell to figure out their gross profit accurately.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>For a retailer, the <strong>Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)</strong> section isn&#039;t just another category. It&#039;s the heart of their financial story. It directly measures the cost of the inventory they&#039;ve sold. This is the only way to understand their true profitability on each product.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>This brings in a whole new set of accounts that a freelancer would never need:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) Accounts:</strong> These live in the 5000s range. A clothing boutique, for example, might have accounts like <strong>5010 - Purchases - Clothing</strong>, <strong>5020 - Purchases - Accessories</strong>, and <strong>5030 - Inbound Freight Costs</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Detailed Revenue Accounts:</strong> They’d want to split their sales to see what’s working. Think <strong>4010 - In-Store Sales</strong>, <strong>4020 - Online Sales</strong>, and a contra-revenue account like <strong>4900 - Sales Returns &amp; Allowances</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Specific Operating Expenses:</strong> Retailers have unique costs that need tracking, such as <strong>6100 - Rent - Retail Space</strong>, <strong>6110 - EFTPOS &amp; Merchant Fees</strong>, and <strong>6120 - Packaging &amp; Shipping Supplies</strong>.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Example for a Service-Based Consultancy</h3>
<p>A consulting firm&#039;s chart of accounts is different again. They don&#039;t have physical inventory. Their main &quot;asset&quot; is their team&#039;s time and expertise. So, the COA needs to be built to track project profitability and the performance of different service offerings.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Service Revenue Streams:</strong> A marketing consultancy would want to see which services are the real money-makers. They&#039;d create distinct income accounts like <strong>4010 - Strategy Consulting Fees</strong>, <strong>4020 - SEO Project Revenue</strong>, and <strong>4030 - Monthly Retainer Income</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Direct Costs:</strong> While it’s not technically COGS, there are direct costs tied to delivering their services. Accounts such as <strong>5010 - Subcontractor - Copywriters</strong> or <strong>5020 - Project-Specific Software</strong> help them calculate the gross profit on each project or client.</li>
<li><strong>Overhead Expenses:</strong> Typical overheads would include <strong>6010 - Salaries &amp; Wages</strong>, <strong>6020 - Professional Development &amp; Training</strong>, and <strong>6030 - Marketing &amp; Advertising</strong>.</li>
</ul>
<p>For any contractor or growing SME in Australia, your chart of accounts is the unsung hero organising your financial data. It&#039;s the numbered ledger framework that makes cloud bookkeeping possible. This is absolutely essential for accurate reporting and tax compliance. This level of organisation is a cornerstone of sound financial management. It mirrors the broader principles that underpin Australia&#039;s economic health, which you can <a href="https://tradingeconomics.com/australia/current-account">learn more about on Trading Economics</a>{:target=&quot;_blank&quot;}.</p>
<h2>Setting Up and Maintaining Your Chart of Accounts</h2>
<p>Your chart of accounts isn&#039;t a &quot;set and forget&quot; document. Think of it as a living part of your business that needs a bit of care to stay useful. A clean, well-organised COA is the bedrock of good financial insight. Keeping it that way takes a little proactive management.</p>
<p>The process really begins when you first set up your accounting software. It continues with regular check-ins to make sure it’s still working for you as your business grows and changes.</p>
<p>The easiest time to get this right is right at the start. You have fewer transactions to worry about. Modern platforms like <a href="https://www.xero.com/au/">Xero</a>{:target=&quot;_blank&quot;} and <a href="https://www.myob.com/au/">MYOB</a>{:target=&quot;_blank&quot;} give you fantastic default templates, but they’re just that. A starting point. The real magic happens when you customise the template to reflect how <em>your</em> business actually operates. This means getting rid of accounts you&#039;ll never use. It also means adding specific ones that give you the insights needed to make smart decisions.</p>
<h3>Best Practices for COA Management</h3>
<p>To stop your chart of accounts from turning into a cluttered, confusing mess, it helps to build a few simple habits. These practices will keep your financial data clean, accurate, and truly representative of what’s happening in your business.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Regular Reviews:</strong> Set aside some time quarterly or even just once a year to look over your COA. As your business evolves, your accounts need to keep up. This is the perfect time to archive old, unused accounts and add new ones for that new service you’ve launched or a new expense category you need to track.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Avoid Getting Too Granular:</strong> It’s tempting to create a new account for every little thing. This almost always leads to a messy, unmanageable list. For instance, instead of having separate accounts for &quot;Pens,&quot; &quot;Paper,&quot; and &quot;Staples,&quot; just group them under a broader &quot;<strong>Office Supplies</strong>&quot; account. Too much detail can actually make it harder to see the bigger picture.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Resist Creating Duplicates:</strong> Before you add a new account, always double-check if a suitable one already exists. Creating duplicate accounts (like having both &quot;Advertising&quot; and &quot;Marketing Spend&quot;) is a common slip-up that splits related costs and makes accurate reporting a nightmare.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>Creating Clear Procedures</h3>
<p>Consistency is everything when it comes to maintaining an effective chart of accounts. Documenting your processes ensures every transaction gets categorised correctly, no matter who&#039;s doing the bookkeeping. For a deeper dive into the operational side of managing financial records, you might find some useful guidance in resources covering <a href="https://usewhale.io/blog/sop-for-accounting-department/">Standard Operating Procedures for an accounting department</a>{:target=&quot;_blank&quot;}.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>A well-maintained COA doesn&#039;t just organise your past transactions. It clarifies your future decisions. Think of it as pruning a garden. Regular maintenance ensures healthy growth and prevents weeds from taking over your financial reports.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>By regularly tidying up your accounts and sticking to clear guidelines, you ensure your COA remains a powerful tool for financial analysis. To simplify your financial management even further, have a look at our other <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/top-small-business-bookkeeping-tips-simplify-your-finances/">top small business bookkeeping tips</a>. These proactive steps will save you a world of time and prevent major headaches when tax time rolls around.</p>
<h2>Common Questions About the Chart of Accounts</h2>
<p>As you get more comfortable with your chart of accounts, it&#039;s natural for specific questions to pop up. Digging into the details is what helps you build a financial structure you can actually trust and use. Let&#039;s tackle some of the most common queries to clear up any confusion.</p>
<h3>How Detailed Should My Chart of Accounts Be?</h3>
<p>The honest answer? It depends entirely on what you need to know to run your business well. There&#039;s no magic number of accounts. But finding the right balance between clarity and complexity is key.</p>
<p>You want enough detail to make smart decisions. But not so much that your day-to-day bookkeeping becomes a chore. A freelance contractor might only need a handful of broad expense categories. On the other hand, a growing retail shop will get huge value from tracking costs by product line or even by store location.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>A good rule of thumb is to only create a new account if tracking that specific item will genuinely change a future business decision. The goal is clarity, not a mountain of administrative work.</p>
</blockquote>
<h3>Can I Change My Chart of Accounts Later?</h3>
<p>Absolutely. In fact, you should. Your chart of accounts isn&#039;t set in stone. Think of it as a living document that needs to evolve right alongside your business.</p>
<p>When you launch a new service, tap into a new revenue stream, or see your expenses shift, you can and should add new accounts to reflect that. Likewise, if an account becomes redundant, you can simply deactivate it. It&#039;s best practice to avoid permanently deleting old accounts with transactions tied to them. This preserves your financial history. Modern accounting software makes it easy to just archive them, which keeps your active list clean without losing any historical data.</p>
<h3>What Is the Difference Between a Chart of Accounts and a General Ledger?</h3>
<p>This is a classic point of confusion, but a simple analogy makes it crystal clear.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Chart of Accounts:</strong> Think of this as the <strong>table of contents</strong> for your financial books. It’s the structured list of all possible categories. The account names and numbers where every transaction could possibly be filed. It&#039;s the framework.</li>
<li><strong>General Ledger:</strong> This is the <strong>book itself</strong>. The general ledger contains the complete, chronological record of every single transaction that has been posted to the accounts listed in your COA.</li>
</ul>
<p>In short, the chart of accounts provides the structure, and the general ledger holds all the detailed stories.</p>
<h3>Is My Accounting Software&#039;s Default COA Good Enough?</h3>
<p>The default chart of accounts you get with software like <a href="https://www.xero.com/au/">Xero</a>{:target=&quot;_blank&quot;} or <a href="https://www.myob.com/au/">MYOB</a>{:target=&quot;_blank&quot;} is a fantastic starting point. But it&#039;s rarely a perfect long-term solution. These templates are built to be generic so they can cater to a massive range of businesses.</p>
<p>This usually means they come loaded with accounts you’ll never touch. They are also missing the specific ones that are crucial for your industry. It’s always worth investing a bit of time upfront to customise it. Go through the default list, archive what&#039;s irrelevant, and add the accounts that will give you real insight into your performance.</p>
<p>Making these tweaks early on is one of the easiest ways to avoid the common <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/bookkeeping-mistakes-small-business-make-what-could-cost-you-time-and-money/">bookkeeping mistakes small businesses make</a>. These mistakes can cost you dearly down the track.</p>

If you need expert help setting up or cleaning up your chart of accounts, our team offers practical advice and hands-on support. Visit us at <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au">https://tnaccounting.com.au</a> to learn how we can make your bookkeeping simpler and more effective.</p>

		<title><![CDATA[What is a Chart of Accounts: Essential Guide for Australian SMEs]]></title>
		<link>https://tnaccounting.com.au/?p=14852</link>

		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Think of a <strong>Chart of Accounts (COA)</strong> as the financial filing system for your business. It&#039;s a complete, organised list of every single account in your general ledger, all logically categorised. This system is the engine that turns your day-to-day transactions into a clear story about your business’s financial health.</p>
<h2>Your Financial Blueprint: What Is a Chart of Accounts?</h2>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdnimg.co/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/7c42e689-189c-49e3-b379-bc82523778a1/what-is-a-chart-of-accounts-accounting-desk.jpg" alt="A &#039;Chart of &#039; document on a desk with a calculator, notebook, pen, and coffee, suggesting financial planning." /></figure></p>
<p>Imagine trying to build a house without a blueprint. You&#039;d have materials scattered everywhere with no real plan for how they all fit together. A business without a Chart of Accounts runs much the same way. Its financial data is disorganised, messy, and almost impossible to make sense of.</p>
<p>The COA acts as a structured index for all your financial activities. Every time money moves in or out of your business, it gets sorted into a specific account. This simple act is what allows you to generate essential financial reports, like your Profit and Loss Statement and Balance Sheet, with just a few clicks.</p>
<h3>The Purpose of a Chart of Accounts</h3>
<p>A well-structured COA does more than just keep things tidy. It’s the very bedrock of reliable financial management and smart decision-making. Here’s why it’s so critical for any Australian small business, from a Melbourne cafe to a sole trader in Beaumaris.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Financial Clarity:</strong> It gives you a clear, at-a-glance overview of your business’s financial position. You can instantly see where your money is coming from and where it’s going.</li>
<li><strong>Accurate Reporting:</strong> A logical COA is non-negotiable for generating accurate financial statements. This is vital for everything from securing a loan and attracting investors to simply understanding your own profitability.</li>
<li><strong>Simplified Tax Compliance:</strong> With dedicated accounts for <strong>GST Collected</strong> and <strong>GST Paid</strong>, preparing your Business Activity Statement (BAS) for the ATO becomes much simpler and less prone to costly errors.</li>
<li><strong>Informed Decisions:</strong> By analysing trends within specific accounts, you can make smarter business choices. For example, you can track your marketing spend against new sales to actually measure your return on investment.</li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>A Chart of Accounts transforms messy bank statements into an organised map of your financial activities. Without one, creating accurate reports is nearly impossible and requires hours of manual work.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Getting your head around your Chart of Accounts is the first step toward building a robust financial foundation. This is absolutely crucial for any business looking to grow, especially if you plan to use a <a href="https://www.statspresso.com/blog/data-analytics-for-small-businesses">guide to data analytics for small businesses</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;}. Ultimately, it’s what gives you real control over your finances.</p>
<h2>The Five Building Blocks of Your Finances</h2>
<p>Every Chart of Accounts, no matter how simple or complex, is built from five fundamental account types. Getting a handle on these categories is the first step to truly mastering your business finances and seeing how everything connects. Think of them as the five essential ingredients in your financial recipe.</p>
<p>Getting these categories right from the start is critical. It makes sure every dollar is sorted correctly, which in turn means your financial reports are accurate and actually useful. Let&#039;s break down each building block with real-world examples for Australian small businesses.</p>
<p>To make this clear, all accounts fall into one of the five categories below. Understanding what each one represents is the key to organising your finances properly.</p>
<h3>The Five Core Account Types Explained</h3>
<h4>Assets</h4>
<ul>
<li><strong>What It Represents:</strong> Everything your business <strong>owns</strong> that has future value.</li>
<li><strong>Example for a Small Business:</strong> Your work ute, cash in the bank, tools, unpaid customer invoices.</li>
</ul>
<h4>Liabilities</h4>
<ul>
<li><strong>What It Represents:</strong> Everything your business <strong>owes</strong> to others.</li>
<li><strong>Example for a Small Business:</strong> A business loan, credit card debt, money owed to suppliers, GST payable to the ATO.</li>
</ul>
<h4>Equity</h4>
<ul>
<li><strong>What It Represents:</strong> The <strong>net worth</strong> of your business (Assets minus Liabilities).</li>
<li><strong>Example for a Small Business:</strong> The money you first put in to start the business (Owner&#039;s Capital) and profits you&#039;ve kept in the company (Retained Earnings).</li>
</ul>
<h4>Revenue</h4>
<ul>
<li><strong>What It Represents:</strong> The <strong>income</strong> you generate from your main business activities.</li>
<li><strong>Example for a Small Business:</strong> Sales from your products, fees for your services, project payments.</li>
</ul>
<h4>Expenses</h4>
<ul>
<li><strong>What It Represents:</strong> The <strong>costs</strong> you incur to earn that revenue.</li>
<li><strong>Example for a Small Business:</strong> Rent for your workshop, staff wages, fuel for the ute, software subscriptions, materials.</li>
</ul>
<p>Now, let&#039;s dig a little deeper into each of these so you can see how they work in practice.</p>
<h3>Assets: What You Own</h3>
<p><strong>Assets</strong> are all the resources your business owns that help you operate and generate income. A simple way to think about them is to list everything of value your company holds that it couldn&#039;t function without. This includes tangible things you can touch and intangible ones you can&#039;t.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Cash in Bank:</strong> This is the most straightforward asset. It’s the money sitting in your business transaction and savings accounts.</li>
<li><strong>Accounts Receivable:</strong> This is the money that customers owe you for goods or services you&#039;ve already delivered but haven&#039;t been paid for yet.</li>
<li><strong>Inventory:</strong> If you run a retail or e-commerce business, this is the value of the products you have on hand, ready to sell.</li>
<li><strong>Equipment:</strong> This covers your work ute, computers, specialised tools, and office furniture. It&#039;s anything necessary for your operations.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Liabilities: What You Owe</h3>
<p><strong>Liabilities</strong> represent what your business owes to other people or organisations. These are your financial obligations or debts that you need to pay back over time. Tracking them accurately is crucial for managing your cash flow and staying out of trouble.</p>
<p>Common liabilities for a small business include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Accounts Payable:</strong> This is the flip side of Accounts Receivable. It&#039;s the money you owe to your suppliers for things you&#039;ve received but haven&#039;t paid for yet, like an invoice from a subcontractor.</li>
<li><strong>Credit Card Balances:</strong> Any outstanding debt on your business credit cards falls into this category.</li>
<li><strong>Business Loans:</strong> This includes any financing you’ve taken on from a bank or lender to fund your operations or buy assets.</li>
<li><strong>GST Payable:</strong> This is the Goods and Services Tax you&#039;ve collected from customers on behalf of the ATO. It&#039;s not your money. You&#039;re just holding it until it&#039;s time to remit it. Understanding how to manage this is key, especially when you learn <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/how-to-lodge-bas-online/">how to lodge your BAS online</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;} with accuracy.</li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>The core relationship in accounting is <strong>Assets = Liabilities + Equity</strong>. This fundamental equation, known as the accounting equation, must always be in balance. It shows that everything the business owns (Assets) is financed by either debt (Liabilities) or the owner&#039;s investment (Equity).</p>
</blockquote>
<h3>Equity: Your Net Worth</h3>
<p><strong>Equity</strong> is essentially the net worth of your business. It’s what would be left over for you, the owner, if you sold all your assets and paid off all your debts. It represents your financial stake in the company.</p>
<p>Equity is made up of a few key things:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Owner&#039;s Capital:</strong> This is the initial cash or other assets you personally invested to get the business off the ground.</li>
<li><strong>Retained Earnings:</strong> These are the cumulative profits the business has earned and kept over the years, rather than being paid out to the owners.</li>
<li><strong>Owner&#039;s Draws:</strong> This is any money you take out of the business for personal use, which naturally reduces your overall equity.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Revenue and Expenses: Your Performance</h3>
<p>Finally, we have the two account types that measure your business&#039;s performance over a specific period, like a month, a quarter, or a financial year.</p>
<p><strong>Revenue:</strong> This is the income your business earns from its primary activities. For a tradie, it’s the money from completing jobs. For a cafe, it’s the sales of coffee and food. It&#039;s the &quot;top line&quot; of your financial reports.</p>
<p><strong>Expenses:</strong> These are all the costs your business racks up in the process of generating that revenue. This covers everything from rent and staff wages to software subscriptions, fuel, and marketing costs. Tracking these properly is how you find ways to save money and boost your profit.</p>
<h2>Structuring Your Chart of Accounts for Clarity</h2>
<p>A logical structure is what turns a simple list of accounts into a powerful business tool. Without a clear system, your financial data can quickly become a disorganised mess, making it nearly impossible to understand what’s really going on. The key to getting that clarity lies in a smart numbering system, a standard practice in accounting software like <a href="https://www.xero.com/au/">Xero</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;} and <a href="https://www.myob.com/au/">MYOB</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;}.</p>
<p>This system organises your finances into a logical hierarchy. Each of the five main account types (Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Revenue, and Expenses) gets its own specific number range. This isn’t just for your accountant’s benefit. It makes your financial reports far more intuitive and easier for anyone in your business to read.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>A well-organised Chart of Accounts tells a clear story. It shows you exactly where your money is, where it came from, and where it went, without you needing to be a financial whiz. This clarity is the foundation for making sound business decisions.</p>
</blockquote>
<h3>How Account Numbering Works</h3>
<p>The numbering convention is surprisingly straightforward and is designed to grow with your business. By grouping similar accounts, you can instantly understand where a transaction fits into your overall financial picture.</p>
<p>Here’s a typical breakdown of the account ranges you’ll see:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>1000s for Assets:</strong> These accounts track everything your business owns. Think of cash in the bank (e.g., <strong>1100</strong>), money owed to you by customers (Accounts Receivable, e.g., <strong>1200</strong>), and physical equipment (e.g., <strong>1500</strong>).</li>
<li><strong>2000s for Liabilities:</strong> This range covers what your business owes to others. It includes bills you need to pay (Accounts Payable, e.g., <strong>2100</strong>), credit card balances (e.g., <strong>2200</strong>), and business loans (e.g., <strong>2500</strong>).</li>
<li><strong>3000s for Equity:</strong> These accounts represent the net worth of your business. This is where you&#039;ll find things like owner’s capital and retained earnings.</li>
<li><strong>4000s for Revenue:</strong> This is where you track all your income. It&#039;s a good idea to have separate accounts for different service types or product sales to see what’s bringing in the most money.</li>
<li><strong>6000s for Expenses:</strong> These accounts capture all your business costs. This is often the most detailed section of your COA, covering everything from rent and utilities to marketing spend.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Using Sub-Accounts for Greater Detail</h3>
<p>The real power of this numbering system comes alive when you use sub-accounts to add more detail. For instance, your main &quot;Marketing&quot; account might be <strong>6100</strong>. You can then create sub-accounts to track specific activities.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>6100</strong> Marketing Expenses (Parent Account)</li>
<li><strong>6110</strong> Social Media Advertising (Sub-account)</li>
<li><strong>6120</strong> Google Ads (Sub-account)</li>
<li><strong>6130</strong> SEO Services (Sub-account)</li>
</ul>
<p>This level of detail lets you see precisely how much you&#039;re spending on each marketing channel, helping you accurately calculate your return on investment. Just as a well-structured COA brings order to your financials, learning to effectively <a href="https://www.guidejar.com/blog/document-business-processes-to-tame-workplace-chaos">document business processes</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;} can bring similar clarity to your entire operation.</p>
<h3>GST Accounts for Australian Businesses</h3>
<p>For any Australian business, correctly setting up Goods and Services Tax (GST) accounts in your COA is non-negotiable. It’s a simple step that makes preparing your Business Activity Statement (BAS) significantly easier and keeps you on the right side of the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).</p>
<p>You should have two specific accounts for this, which usually sit in the Liabilities section:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>GST Collected (Liability):</strong> This account tracks the <strong>10%</strong> GST you’ve collected on sales. Remember, this is money you’re holding for the ATO.</li>
<li><strong>GST Paid (Asset/Contra-Liability):</strong> This account tracks the GST you’ve paid on your business purchases. This is the amount you can claim back as a credit from the ATO.</li>
</ul>
<p>Since GST reporting became mandatory, businesses using digital COAs have seen huge benefits. In fact, Australian businesses that embraced cloud accounting tools have historically seen a significant reduction in tax adjustment penalties. For more context on this, you can review the <a href="https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/economy/national-accounts/australian-national-accounts-state-accounts/latest-release">latest national accounts data</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;} from the Australian Bureau of Statistics to see how digital tools have impacted business accounting.</p>
<h2>Chart of Accounts Examples for Australian Businesses</h2>
<p>Theory is one thing, but seeing a Chart of Accounts (COA) in action is what really makes the concept click. The right structure depends entirely on your business, as different operations have very different financial stories to tell. A well-organised COA helps you track exactly what matters most to your success.</p>
<p>To help you visualise this, let&#039;s move from abstract ideas to concrete examples. We&#039;ll explore some practical, simplified templates for common Australian business structures to show you what a real-world COA actually looks like.</p>
<p>The diagram below shows how different account categories fit into a clear hierarchy, from high-level assets down to specific expenses.</p>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdnimg.co/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/50afbb93-5083-44ea-a70b-84a4e8021478/what-is-a-chart-of-accounts-coa-hierarchy.jpg" alt="A hierarchical diagram illustrating a Chart of Accounts (COA) structure from Assets to Expenses and Marketing." /></figure></p>
<p>This is how a COA organises your financial data logically. It lets you drill down from broad categories like <strong>Assets</strong> into granular details, such as specific <strong>Marketing</strong> expenses.</p>
<h3>For a Sole Trader or Contractor</h3>
<p>For a sole trader, the COA is usually pretty straightforward. The main goal is to create a clear distinction between business finances and any personal use of funds so you can accurately track income and deductible expenses for tax time.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Simplicity is key:</strong> The structure is lean and avoids unnecessary complexity. It’s designed for easy management by one person.</li>
<li><strong>Key accounts include:</strong><ul>
<li><strong>Revenue:</strong> A single account like &quot;Professional Fees&quot; or &quot;Consulting Income&quot; is often all you need.</li>
<li><strong>Expenses:</strong> You’ll want specific accounts for common costs like &quot;Software Subscriptions,&quot; &quot;Home Office Expenses,&quot; and &quot;Motor Vehicle Expenses&quot; to make sure you’re maximising your tax deductions.</li>
<li><strong>Equity:</strong> The &quot;<strong>Owner&#039;s Drawings</strong>&quot; account is vital. It tracks any money you take out of the business for personal use, keeping your business and personal funds cleanly separated.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>For a Retail Business</h3>
<p>A retail business&#039;s COA is naturally more detailed. It has a strong focus on inventory, sales, and the cost of selling physical products. After all, managing stock is the lifeblood of retail, and the COA has to reflect that.</p>
<p>This structure allows for a clear calculation of your gross profit on every single item you sell.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Inventory focus:</strong> Your COA must accurately track the value of all the products you have on your shelves.</li>
<li><strong>Key accounts include:</strong><ul>
<li><strong>Revenue:</strong> &quot;<strong>Sales Revenue</strong>&quot; is the primary income account here.</li>
<li><strong>Cost of Goods Sold (COGS):</strong> This is a critical expense category. It directly tracks the cost of the inventory you&#039;ve sold. Without it, you can&#039;t calculate your gross margin.</li>
<li><strong>Assets:</strong> The &quot;<strong>Inventory Asset</strong>&quot; account represents the value of stock you own but haven’t sold yet.</li>
<li><strong>Expenses:</strong> You’ll need specific accounts for costs like &quot;Shop Rent,&quot; &quot;Staff Wages,&quot; and &quot;EFTPOS Fees&quot; to track the unique expenses of running a retail store.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>For a Service-Based Business</h3>
<p>This COA template is designed to highlight different revenue streams and the costs associated with delivering your services. If you run a business like a marketing agency or a design studio, tracking project profitability is everything.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Revenue stream tracking:</strong> This structure helps you understand which of your services are the most profitable.</li>
<li><strong>Key accounts include:</strong><ul>
<li><strong>Revenue:</strong> Having separate accounts like &quot;Retainer Income&quot; and &quot;Project-Based Income&quot; allows for a much more detailed analysis of your business model.</li>
<li><strong>Cost of Sales:</strong> &quot;<strong>Subcontractor Costs</strong>&quot; is a key account for tracking payments to freelancers or other agencies you partner with to deliver work for your clients.</li>
<li><strong>Expenses:</strong> Detailed accounts like &quot;Client Entertainment&quot; and &quot;Specific Software&quot; (e.g., Adobe Creative Cloud) give you deeper insights into your operational spending.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h2>Setting Up Your COA in Cloud Accounting Software</h2>
<p><figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://cdnimg.co/413aa6a2-4925-4343-93c8-fe8d0c5f2c8d/a372e7e8-0ede-4f57-9430-fcf7562261ab/what-is-a-chart-of-accounts-chart-of-accounts.jpg" alt="A person using a laptop displaying a chart of accounts for financial management, with a notebook on a white desk." /></figure></p>
<p>Alright, let&#039;s get practical. Setting up your Chart of Accounts (COA) in modern cloud accounting software is much more straightforward than you might imagine. Platforms like Xero and MYOB hand you a default template right out of the box, which is a fantastic starting point.</p>
<p>Think of that default COA like a pre-built house frame. It’s got the essential structure, but it’s up to you to put up the walls, hang the windows, and add the finishes that make it <em>your</em> home. Your job is to take that template and customise it until it perfectly mirrors your business’s unique financial activity. A great first step is to check out our guide on the <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/best-accounting-software-for-small-business-australia/">best accounting software for small businesses in Australia</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;} to pick the right platform for you.</p>
<h3>Customising Your Default COA</h3>
<p>Once you’ve got your software’s default COA loaded, it’s time to start customising. This process is all about adding, hiding, and tweaking accounts to build a financial map that’s both detailed enough to be useful and simple enough to read at a glance.</p>
<p>Here are a few actionable tips to get you started:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Add Industry-Specific Accounts:</strong> If you run a retail shop, you absolutely need a &quot;Cost of Goods Sold&quot; account. A consulting firm, on the other hand, will probably need one for &quot;Subcontractor Fees.&quot; Add accounts that truly reflect how your business makes and spends its money.</li>
<li><strong>Hide Unused Accounts:</strong> Default templates are built to be comprehensive, but you won&#039;t need every single account. Hiding or archiving what you don’t use declutters your workspace, making it far easier to code transactions accurately and reducing the risk of errors.</li>
<li><strong>Maintain Consistent Naming:</strong> Use clear, consistent names for your accounts. Vague titles like &quot;Miscellaneous&quot; or &quot;Other&quot; should be used very sparingly. When your reports are easy to understand, you&#039;re more likely to make smarter decisions.</li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>One of the most common mistakes I see business owners make is creating way too many accounts. While detail is good, getting too granular makes reports long, confusing, and ultimately, useless. The goal is clarity, not complexity.</p>
</blockquote>
<h3>Avoiding Common Pitfalls</h3>
<p>Taking a proactive approach to your COA setup will save you from painful and expensive cleanups down the track. For most businesses, a well-organised COA is the key to managing compliance and unlocking growth. Smart planning helps you dodge common traps like unallocated GST, an issue that trips up a significant number of businesses with their quarterly BAS lodgements.</p>
<p>While you can certainly set up a COA on your own, getting an accountant involved from day one is a seriously smart investment. An expert can help ensure your structure is optimised for tax efficiency and is scalable enough to grow with your business, saving you from a world of headaches later on.</p>
<h2>Maintaining a Healthy Chart of Accounts</h2>
<p>Your Chart of Accounts isn’t a “set and forget” document. Think of it more like a garden. It needs regular attention to stay organised, accurate, and useful. A neglected COA can quickly get overgrown with messy, duplicated, or old accounts, making your financial data completely unreliable.</p>
<p>Consider it part of your financial fitness routine. Consistent maintenance keeps your business’s financial backbone strong, giving you the stability needed for trustworthy reports and smart growth. This proactive approach turns your COA from a simple list into a truly powerful management tool.</p>
<h3>Best Practices for COA Maintenance</h3>
<p>Building good habits around your Chart of Accounts is crucial. These practices will stop small issues from snowballing into massive clean-up projects, saving you a headache and a whole lot of money down the track.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Schedule Regular Reviews:</strong> Set aside some time every quarter, or at the very least once a year, to go through your entire COA. This is the perfect chance to archive old accounts you’re no longer using and figure out if new ones are needed as your business changes.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Resist On-the-Fly Changes:</strong> It’s tempting to create a new account every time a unique expense pops up, but this is a fast track to clutter. Instead, have a clear process for adding or changing accounts, which should probably involve a quick chat with your bookkeeper or accountant first.</p>
</li>
<li><p><strong>Train Your Team:</strong> If you have staff who code transactions, make sure they actually understand your COA. Consistent and accurate coding is the bedrock of data integrity. A small investment in training can prevent widespread <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au/bookkeeping-mistakes-small-business-make-what-could-cost-you-time-and-money/">bookkeeping mistakes that cost small businesses</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;} and protect your finances.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>The Benefits of a Clean COA</h3>
<p>Keeping your Chart of Accounts tidy isn&#039;t just about good housekeeping. It delivers real, tangible benefits that directly impact your bottom line and your ability to make decisions.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>A clean, well-maintained COA is your ticket to reliable financial data, smoother tax seasons, and the strategic insights you need to grow your business confidently. It transforms your accounting from a compliance task into a strategic asset.</p>
</blockquote>
<p><strong>Clearer Financial Insights:</strong> With an organised COA, your financial reports become incredibly clear and easy to understand. You can quickly analyse spending, track different revenue streams, and spot trends without having to dig through a messy list of confusing accounts.</p>
<p><strong>Smoother Tax Preparation:</strong> When it’s time to lodge your BAS or end-of-year tax return, a tidy COA makes the process infinitely faster and less stressful. Your accountant can easily find the numbers they need, which almost always translates to lower accounting fees for you.</p>
<h2>Chart of Accounts FAQs</h2>
<p>We’ve walked through the fundamentals of what a chart of accounts is, but let&#039;s be honest, that&#039;s where the real-world questions usually start. Here are a few common ones that business owners often ask.</p>
<h3>How Many Accounts Should My COA Have?</h3>
<p>There&#039;s no magic number here. The right amount of accounts really comes down to the size and complexity of your business.</p>
<ul>
<li>A <strong>sole trader</strong> just starting out might only need <strong>30-50 accounts</strong> to get a clear picture of their finances.</li>
<li>On the other hand, a growing <strong>retail business</strong> could easily have over <strong>200 accounts</strong> to properly track different inventory types, sales channels, and specific costs.</li>
</ul>
<p>The goal is to strike a balance. You want enough detail to generate useful reports that help you make decisions, but not so much that it becomes a confusing mess. A good starting point is the default template in your accounting software. Only add new accounts when you genuinely need them.</p>
<h3>Can I Change My Chart of Accounts Later?</h3>
<p>Yes, and you absolutely should! Your COA isn&#039;t set in stone. It&#039;s a living document that needs to grow and change right alongside your business. As you add new services, expand into new locations, or incur new types of expenses, you’ll need to add accounts to track them.</p>
<p>But there&#039;s one golden rule: <strong>never delete old accounts</strong> that have transactions recorded against them. Deleting an account with a history is like tearing a chapter out of your business&#039;s financial story. It can corrupt your historical data and make a mess of your reports. Instead, just make the old, unused accounts inactive. A yearly review with your accountant is the perfect time to clean things up and make sure your COA still fits.</p>
<h3>What Is the Difference Between a COA and a General Ledger?</h3>
<p>This is a great question, and an analogy helps make it clear. Think of your accounting system as a book.</p>
<ul>
<li>The <strong>Chart of Accounts</strong> is the <em>table of contents</em>. It’s a neat, organised list of all the possible categories (your accounts) where financial information can be filed. It provides the structure.</li>
<li>The <strong>General Ledger</strong> is the <em>book itself</em>. It has all the pages filled with detailed entries. It’s the complete, chronological record of every single transaction that has happened within each of those accounts.</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<p>A well-structured chart of accounts is your first step towards real financial clarity. For expert guidance on setting up and maintaining a COA that supports your growth, the team at <strong>Trew North Accounting</strong> is here to help. <a href="https://tnaccounting.com.au">Discover our business accounting services</a>{target=&quot;_blank&quot;}.</p>
